entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.17.1-Josh.17.6">Jos 17:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen2907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2908" type="x-p"/> Before proceeding to the more detailed description of the inheritance, the historian thinks it necessary to observe that the Manassites received a double inheritance. This remark is introduced with the words “<hi type="italic">for he was the first-born of Joseph</hi>.” On this account, in addition to the territory already given to him in Gilead and Bashan, he received a second allotment of territory in Canaan proper. With the word למכיר (for Machir) the more minute account of the division of the Manassites commences. וגו למכיר is first of all written absolutely at the beginning of the sentence, and then resumed in לו ויהי: “<hi type="italic">to Machir, the first-born of Manasseh ... to him were Gilead and Bashan assigned, because he was a man of war</hi>,” i.e., a warlike man, and had earned for himself a claim to the inheritance of Gilead and Bashan through the peculiar bravery which he had displayed in the conquest of those lands. By <hi type="italic">Machir</hi>, however, we are not to understand the actual son of Manasseh, but his family; and הגּלעד אבי does not mean “father of Gilead,” but <hi type="italic">lord</hi> (possessor) <hi type="italic">of Gilead</hi>, for Machir’s son Gilead is always called גלעד without the article (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.17.3">Jos 17:3</reference>; Num 26:29-30; Num 27:1; Num 36:1; <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.17">1Ch 7:17</reference>), whereas the country of that name is just as constantly called הגּלעד (see <reference osisRef="Josh.17.1">Jos 17:1</reference>, the last clause, <reference osisRef="Josh.17.5">Jos 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.11">Jos 13:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.31">Jos 13:31</reference>; Num 32:40; Deu 3:10.). “<hi type="italic">And there came</hi>, i.e., the lot fell (the lot is to be repeated from <reference osisRef="Josh.17.1">Jos 17:1</reference>), <hi type="italic">to the other descendants of Manasseh according to their families</hi>,” which are then enumerated as in Num 26:30-32. “<hi type="italic">These are the male descendants of Manasseh</hi>.” הזּכרים must not be altered, notwithstanding the fact that it is preceded and followed by הגּותרים; it is evidently used deliberately as an antithesis to the female descendants of Manasseh mentioned in Jos 17:3.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.17.7-Josh.17.11">Jos 17:7-11</reference> <hi type="italic">Boundaries and extent of the inheritance of the ten families of Manasseh</hi>. - <reference osisRef="Josh.17.7-Josh.17.10">Jos 17:7-10</reference>, the southern boundary, which coincides with the northern boundary of Ephraim described in <reference osisRef="Josh.16.6-Josh.16.8">Jos 16:6-8</reference>, and is merely given here with greater precision in certain points. It went “<hi type="italic">from Asher to Michmethah, before Shechem</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Asher</hi> is not the territory of the tribe of Asher, but a distinct locality; according to the <hi type="italic">Onom.</hi> (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> <hi type="italic">Asher</hi>) a place on the high road from Neapolis to Scythopolis, fifteen Roman miles from the former. It is not to be found, however, in the ruins of Tell <hi type="italic">Um el Aschera</hi> (<hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>) or Tell <hi type="italic">Um Ajra</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> Bibl. Res. pp. 310, 327), an hour to the south of Beisan, as <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> supposes, but in the village of Yasir, where there are magnificent ruins, about five hours and ten minutes from Nabulus on the road to Beisan (<hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>, Mem. pp. 237, 289; R. ii. p. 295). <hi type="italic">Michmethah</hi>, before Shechem, is still unknown (see <reference osisRef="Josh.16.6">Jos 16:6</reference>). Shechem was founded by the Hivite prince Shechem (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.18">Gen 33:18</reference>), and is frequently mentioned in the book of Genesis. It stood between Ebal and Gerizim, was given up by Ephraim to the Levites, and declared a free city (city of refuge: <reference osisRef="Josh.21.21">Jos 21:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.20.7">Jos 20:7</reference>). It was there that the ten tribes effected their separation from Judah 1Ki 12:1.), and Jeroboam resided there (1Ki 12:25). In later times it was the chief city of the country of Samaria, and the capital of the Samaritans (Joh 4:5); and the name of <hi type="italic">Neapolis</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Flavia Neapolis</hi>, from which the present <hi type="italic">Nabulus</hi> or <hi type="italic">Nablus</hi> has come, was given to it in honour of Vespasian (see <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 161ff.). From this point the boundary went אל־היּמין (i.e., either “<hi type="italic">to the right side</hi>,” the south side, or <hi type="italic">to Yamin</hi>), “<hi type="italic">To the inhabitants of En-tappuah</hi>.” Whether <hi type="italic">Yamin</hi> is an appellative or a proper name is doubtful. But even if it be the name of a place, it is quite certain that it cannot be the village of <hi type="italic">Yamôn</hi>, an hour to the south-east of <hi type="italic">Taanuk</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. pp. 161, 167, etc.), as this is much too far north, and, judging from <reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>, belonged to the territory of Asher. In the case of <hi type="italic">En-tappuah</hi>, the inhabitants are mentioned instead of the district, because the district belonged to Manasseh, whilst the town on the border of Manasseh was given to the Ephraimites. The situation of the town has not yet been discovered: see at Jos 16:8. From this point the boundary ran down to the Cane-brook (see <reference osisRef="Josh.16.8">Jos 16:8</reference>), namely to the south side of the brook. <div eID="gen2909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2910" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">These towns were assigned to Ephraim in the midst of the towns of Manasseh, and</hi> (but) <hi type="italic">the territory of Manasseh was on the north of the brook</hi>.” The only possible meaning of these words is the following: From Tappuah, the boundary went down to the Cane-brook and crossed it, so that the south side of the brook really belonged to the territory of Manasseh; nevertheless the towns on this south side were allotted to Ephraim, whilst only the territory to the north of the brook fell to the lot of the Manassites. This is expressed more plainly in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.17.10">Jos 17:10</reference></hi>: “<hi type="italic">To the south (of the brook the land came) to Ephraim, and to the north to Manasseh</hi>.” In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Josh.17.10">Jos 17:10</reference></hi> the northern and eastern boundaries are only briefly indicated: “<hi type="italic">And they</hi> (the Manassites) <hi type="italic">touched Asher towards the north, and Issachar towards the east</hi>.” The reason why this boundary was not described more minutely, was probably because it had not yet been fixed. For (<reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>) Manasseh also received towns and districts in (within the territory of) Issachar and Asher, viz., Beth-shean, etc. <hi type="italic">Beth-shean</hi>, to the wall of which Saul’s body was fastened (1Sa 31:10.; <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.12">2Sa 21:12</reference>), was afterwards called <hi type="italic">Scythopolis</hi>. It was in the valley of the Jordan, where the plain of Jezreel slopes off into the valley; its present name is <hi type="italic">Beisan</hi>, a place where there are considerable ruins of great antiquity, about two hours from the Jordan (vid., <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. pp. 162ff.; <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 174; Bibl. Res. p. 325; <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 150-1). This city, with its daughter towns, was in the territory of Issachar, which was on the east of Manasseh, and may have extended a considerable distance towards the south along the valley of the Jordan, as the territory of Manasseh and Ephraim did not run into the valley of the Jordan; but Asher (Yasir) is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.17.7">Jos 17:7</reference> as the most easterly place in Manasseh, and, according to <reference osisRef="Josh.16.6-Josh.16.7">Jos 16:6-7</reference>, the eastern boundary of Ephraim ran down along the eastern edge of the mountains as far as Jericho, without including the Jordan valley. At the same time, the Ghor on the western side of the Jordan below Beisan, as far as the plain of Jericho, was of no great value to any tribe, as this district, according to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (de Bell. Jud. iv. 8, 2, and iii. 10, 7), was uninhabited because of its barrenness. The other towns, <hi type="italic">Ibleam</hi>, etc., with the exception of Endor perhaps, were in the territory of Asher, and almost all on the south-west border of the plain of Esdraelon. <hi type="italic">Ibleam</hi>, called <hi type="italic">Bileam</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.55">1Ch 6:55</reference> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.70">70</reference>), a Levitical town (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.21.25">Jos 21:25</reference>), was not very far from Megiddo (2Ki 9:27), and has probably been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Khirbet-Belameh</hi>, half an hour to the south of Jenin; according to <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi>, it is the same place as <hi type="italic">Belamon</hi>, <hi type="italic">Belmen</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Belthem</hi> (Judith 4:4; 7:3; 8:3). With דאר ואת־ישׁבי the construction changes, so that there is an anacolouthon, which can be explained, however, on the ground that ל היה may not only mean to be assigned to, but also to receive or to have. In this last sense ואת is attached. The inhabitants are mentioned instead of the towns, because the historian had already the thought present in his mind, that the Manassites were unable to exterminate the Canaanites from the towns allotted to them. <hi type="italic">Dor</hi> is the present <hi type="italic">Tortura</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.2">Jos 11:2</reference>). <hi type="italic">Endor</hi>, the home of the witch (<reference osisRef="1Sam.28.7">1Sa 28:7</reference>), four Roman miles to the south of Tabor (<hi type="italic">Onom.</hi>), at present a village called <hi type="italic">Endôr</hi>, on the northern shoulder of the Duhy or Little Hermon (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 225; Bibl. Res. p. 340). <hi type="italic">Taanach</hi> and <hi type="italic">Megiddo</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Taanuk</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lejun</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.12.21">Jos 12:21</reference>). The three last towns, with the places dependent upon them, are connected more closely together by הנּפת שׁלשׁת, the three-hill-country, probably because they formed a common league.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Josh.17.14-Josh.17.18">Jos 17:14-18</reference> <hi type="italic">Complaint of the Descendants of Joseph respecting the inheritance allotted to them</hi>. - Jos 17:14. As the descendants of Joseph formed two tribes (Ephraim and Manasseh), they gave utterance to their dissatisfaction that Joshua had given them (“<hi type="italic">me</hi>,” the house of Joseph, <reference osisRef="Josh.17.17">Jos 17:17</reference>) but one lot, but one portion (חבל, a measure, then the land measured off), for an inheritance, although they were a strong and numerous people. “<hi type="italic">So far hath Jehovah blessed me hitherto</hi>.” עד־אשׁד, to this (sc., numerous people), is to be understood <hi type="italic">de gradu</hi>; עד־כּה, hitherto, <hi type="italic">de tempore</hi>. There was no real ground for this complaint. As Ephraim numbered only 32,500 and Manasseh 52,700 at the second census in the time of Moses (Num 26), and therefore Ephraim and half Manasseh together did not amount to more than 58,000 or 59,000, this tribe and a half were not so strong as Judah with its 76,500, and were even weaker than Dan with its 64,400, or Issachar with its 64,300 men, and therefore could not justly lay claim to more than the territory of a single tribe. Moreover, the land allotted to them was in one of the most fertile parts of Palestine. For although as a whole the mountains of Ephraim have much the same character as those of Judah, yet the separate mountains are neither so rugged nor so lofty, there being only a few of them that reach the height of 2500 feet above the level of the sea (see <hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xv. pp. 475ff.; <hi type="italic">V. de Velde</hi>, Mem. pp. 177ff.); moreover, they are intersected by many broad valleys and fertile plateaux, which are covered with fruitful fields and splendid plantations of olives,vines, and fig trees (see <hi type="italic">Rob.</hi> iii. p. 78, Bibl. Res. pp. 290ff.; <hi type="italic">Seetzen</hi>, ii. pp. 165ff., 190ff.). On the west the mountains slope off into the hill country, which joins the plain of Sharon, with its invariable fertility. “The soil here is a black clay soil of unfathomable depth, which is nearly all ploughed, and is of such unusual fertility that a cultivated plain here might furnish an almost unparalleled granary for the whole land. Interminable fields full of wheat and barley with their waving ears, which were very nearly ripe, with here and there a field of millet, that was already being diligently reaped by the peasants, presented a glorious sight” (<hi type="italic">Ritter</hi>, Erdk. xvi. pp. 567-8).
